why-rag-grounding.text: Support asks the model "what is our current refund window?" and it confidently answers "14 days" — the number from its training data, not your policy page, which changed to 30 last quarter. Nobody can tell the answer is stale because it was never tied to a source. RAG fixes this by making the answer come FROM a retrieved passage you control, not from frozen weights. This lesson makes that distinction concrete.

A base LLM answers from PARAMETRIC memory — facts baked into its weights at training time, frozen and unattributable. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al., 2020) adds NON-PARAMETRIC memory: a searchable index of your documents. At query time you retrieve the relevant passages and put them in the prompt, so the answer is grounded in text you can cite, update, and audit. That is the whole point: fresh facts, private facts, and citations — none of which a frozen model can give you.

why-rag-grounding.reveal: (a) needs retrieval: it depends on a private, changeable fact the model was never trained on (and if it were, it would be stale). (b) is self-contained general knowledge — retrieval adds cost and latency for nothing. RAG is for fact-dependent, fresh, or private questions; do not route everything through it.

why-rag-grounding.commonMistake: Believing RAG "teaches" the model new facts. It does not touch the weights — it puts retrieved text in the prompt at inference time. If retrieval returns nothing relevant, a RAG system is exactly as ignorant as the base model, just slower.

why-rag-grounding.text: The RAG paper (Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020) frames a language system as two memories. PARAMETRIC memory is the seq2seq model's weights — everything it learned at training, frozen and unattributable; you cannot update it without retraining and it cannot cite a source. NON-PARAMETRIC memory is an external index (in the paper, a dense vector index of Wikipedia read by a DPR retriever) that you CAN edit at any time. RAG retrieves relevant passages for the query and conditions generation on them. The paper gives two formulations: RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved passages for the whole output; RAG-Token may attend to different passages per generated token. The engineering payoff is not raw intelligence — it is that the answer becomes GROUNDED: tied to specific retrieved text you can update (fix a stale policy by editing one document), attribute (cite the span), and audit (see exactly what the model was told). A frozen model memorizes; a RAG system grounds. When retrieval fails to surface the relevant passage, grounding fails — which is why the rest of this course is about retrieval QUALITY, not just plumbing.

loaders-cleaning.outcome: Normalize raw source text before it is chunked and embedded: strip boilerplate, collapse whitespace, and drop empty fragments so the index holds signal, not noise.
loaders-cleaning.doNotClaim: Don't claim cleaning is cosmetic — nav bars, repeated headers, and blank runs become embedded vectors that pollute every future search.

loaders-cleaning.text: A RAG bot keeps retrieving the same "Skip to main content · Cookie settings · © 2026" fragment for unrelated questions. Someone loaded raw HTML dumps straight into the index, so the site chrome got embedded as if it were content and now out-competes real passages. The fix is upstream cleaning. This lesson makes ingestion hygiene a concrete, testable step.

Before any embedding happens, raw sources (HTML, PDF text, Markdown, scraped pages) must be loaded and CLEANED. Real documents carry boilerplate: navigation, cookie banners, repeated headers/footers, page numbers, and runs of blank lines. Every one of those, if left in, becomes a chunk and then a vector that can be retrieved. Cleaning is not formatting for humans — it is removing text that would produce misleading matches. Do it once at ingestion and the whole downstream pipeline gets cleaner.

loaders-cleaning.prompt: Before reading: you scrape 500 web pages and embed the raw text. Why might a search for "refund policy" return a page's footer instead of its body?
loaders-cleaning.reveal: Because the footer ("Refunds · Terms · Privacy") was embedded as a chunk and its words overlap the query. Boilerplate that repeats across pages gets a strong, generic vector that matches many queries. Strip repeated chrome at ingestion so only real content is indexed.

loaders-cleaning.intro: A minimal cleaning pass: normalize whitespace, drop boilerplate lines, and remove empties before chunking.
steps: Collapse runs of whitespace/newlines so spacing does not fragment text.
Drop empty lines — an empty chunk is a wasted, noisy vector.
Remove known boilerplate (nav, cookie, copyright, page numbers) by pattern.
Do it ONCE at ingestion so every chunk and embedding downstream is clean.
loaders-cleaning.commonMistake: Cleaning for display (fixing capitalization, prettifying) instead of cleaning for retrieval (removing text that produces bad matches). The index does not care if text is pretty; it cares that boilerplate is gone.

loaders-cleaning.text: Ingestion is the first quality gate in a RAG pipeline, and it is unforgiving: anything you load becomes a chunk, every chunk becomes an embedding, and every embedding is retrievable forever until you re-index. So the cleaning pass has one job — remove text that would create MISLEADING matches. Three moves cover most of it. (1) Normalize whitespace: PDFs and HTML produce ragged spacing and hard line breaks mid-sentence; collapsing them keeps a sentence together so it chunks and embeds as one idea. (2) Drop empties: a blank or near-blank chunk still gets a vector, and near-identical empty vectors cluster and surface as false matches. (3) Strip boilerplate: navigation, cookie banners, repeated headers/footers, "Page 3 of 12" — this text repeats across hundreds of documents, so it earns a strong generic embedding that out-competes real content for many queries. The discipline is "garbage in, garbage embedded": you cannot fix a polluted index with a better prompt or a bigger top-k, only by re-cleaning and re-ingesting. Clean once, correctly, at the boundary.
loaders-cleaning.title: The index only holds what you let in
The ingestion cleaning gate
loaders-cleaning.subtitle: raw source normalized before it can be embedded

storyboard.say: Everything begins at the raw source — HTML, PDF text, Markdown, scraped pages — loaded before any embedding can happen.
First move: normalize whitespace. Ragged spacing and mid-sentence line breaks collapse so a sentence stays whole and embeds as one idea.
Now the key decision: is this line real content, or is it navigation, cookie banners, and repeated headers — site chrome?
Chrome that fails the test is discarded, looped back out of the pipeline so it never becomes a retrievable vector.
Kept lines advance, but a second filter drops empties — blank chunks still get vectors that cluster into false matches.
Only non-empty signal survives into clean lines, ready to be chunked and embedded as real passages.
The insight: ingestion is an unforgiving quality gate — anything you load becomes retrievable forever, so cleaning upstream is the fix.

chunking-strategies.proof: A chunker that turns a token stream into fixed-size overlapping windows, with an assertable chunk count and correct boundaries.
chunking-strategies.unlock: You can compute chunk count from length, size, and stride, and explain why overlap prevents boundary loss.
chunking-strategies.outcome: Split cleaned text into fixed-size chunks with a controlled overlap, and predict exactly how many chunks a given size/overlap produces.
chunking-strategies.doNotClaim: Don't claim there is one right chunk size — it trades retrieval precision against context completeness, and overlap is what saves facts that straddle a boundary.

chunking-strategies.text: A user asks "what is the cancellation fee after 30 days?" and the answer is wrong. The relevant sentence was split across two chunks — "...a cancellation fee of" ended one chunk and "$50 applies after 30 days" started the next — so neither chunk alone contained the fact, and neither retrieved well. Overlap exists precisely for this. This lesson makes chunk size and overlap a number you can compute and defend.

Embeddings work on chunks, not whole documents: a document is too long for one meaningful vector, so you split it. The two knobs are SIZE (how much text per chunk) and OVERLAP (how much consecutive chunks share). Bigger chunks carry more context but blur precision (the vector averages many ideas); smaller chunks are precise but can cut a fact in half. Overlap is the fix for the cut: by repeating the last N tokens of one chunk at the start of the next, a fact that straddles a boundary survives whole in at least one chunk.

chunking-strategies.prompt: Before reading: you split 1000 tokens into chunks of size 200 with overlap 50. How many chunks, and why is it more than 1000/200 = 5?
chunking-strategies.reveal: The stride (advance per chunk) is size − overlap = 150, not 200. Chunks start at 0,150,300,...; count = ceil((1000 − 200)/150) + 1 = ceil(800/150)+1 = 6+1 = 7. Overlap makes chunks advance slower than their size, so you get MORE chunks than naive length/size — that is the cost of overlap.

chunking-strategies.intro: A fixed-size chunker with overlap, and the formula for how many chunks it yields.
steps: Choose size (context per chunk) and overlap (shared tokens between neighbors).
Stride = size − overlap; that is how far each chunk starts after the last.
A fact that straddles a boundary appears whole in the overlapping region of one chunk.
Chunk count grows as overlap grows — more redundancy costs more vectors to store and search.
chunking-strategies.commonMistake: Setting overlap equal to or greater than size. Stride becomes zero or negative, the loop never advances (or moves backward), and you produce infinite/duplicate chunks. Overlap must be strictly less than size.

chunking-strategies.text: A chunk is the unit of retrieval: you embed chunks and retrieve chunks, so how you cut the document decides what can be found. Fixed-size chunking slides a window of SIZE tokens across the text, advancing by STRIDE = size − overlap each step. Size sets a tension: LARGE chunks preserve context (the whole paragraph around a fact) but their single embedding averages many ideas, so it matches queries less sharply — precision drops. SMALL chunks give a crisp, specific vector but risk cutting a fact in half, so neither half retrieves. OVERLAP resolves the seam problem: by repeating the last `overlap` tokens of a chunk at the start of the next, any fact spanning a boundary lands intact inside at least one chunk's window. The price is redundancy — smaller stride means more chunks, so more vectors to embed, store, and search, and the same sentence may retrieve twice. The count is deterministic: for N tokens with N > size, you get ceil((N − size) / stride) + 1 chunks. There is no universal best size; it is a per-corpus decision you tune against retrieval metrics (recall@k, later in this course), but the mechanics — stride, boundaries, count — are exact and worth being able to compute in your head.
chunking-strategies.title: Chunking trades precision against completeness, and overlap patches the seams
Fixed-size chunking with overlap
chunking-strategies.subtitle: stride = size − overlap; the shared region saves boundary facts

storyboard.say: Embeddings work on chunks, not whole documents, so we start with cleaned tokens and slide a fixed-size window across them.
Each window grabs SIZE tokens of text, then advances by a stride to place the next window.
The key knob: stride equals size minus overlap, so a larger overlap means the window advances less each step.
That advance repeats the tail: the last overlap tokens of one chunk reappear at the start of the next.
The shared region is the fix for split facts, a cancellation fee sentence cut across a boundary now lands intact in one chunk.
Each window emits into the chunk set, the units you actually embed and retrieve, so how you cut decides what can be found.

metadata-provenance.proof: A chunk builder that emits records carrying source + span metadata, and a filter that selects only chunks from an allowed source set.
metadata-provenance.unlock: You can list the provenance fields a chunk needs and explain how each enables citation, filtering, or freshness.
metadata-provenance.outcome: Attach provenance to every chunk (source id, title, section, char span, timestamp) so a retrieved chunk can be cited, filtered, and traced back to its exact origin.
metadata-provenance.doNotClaim: Don't claim the chunk text is enough — without provenance you cannot cite a span, filter by source, or expire stale content, and the answer becomes untraceable.

metadata-provenance.text: Legal asks "which document and section does this answer come from?" and the team cannot say — the pipeline stored only chunk text and embeddings, no source, no offsets. Every answer is now an unverifiable assertion. Provenance is the metadata that turns a retrieved chunk back into a citable, filterable, expirable fact. This lesson makes it a required field, not an afterthought.

A chunk is not just text — it is text FROM somewhere. Provenance metadata (source document id, title, section heading, the character span within the source, and an ingest/updated timestamp) travels with the chunk into the index. It powers three things you will need in later lessons: CITATION (point the user at the exact source span), FILTERING (restrict retrieval to allowed sources, a tenant, or a date range — done in the vector store as a metadata filter), and FRESHNESS (expire or re-rank stale chunks by timestamp). Skip it at ingestion and you cannot add it later without re-indexing.

metadata-provenance.prompt: Before reading: your bot answers a question but a user asks "where did you get that?". What minimum metadata must the chunk carry for you to answer precisely?
metadata-provenance.reveal: At minimum: the source document id/title and the character span (start,end) within that source, so you can quote and link the exact passage. A timestamp lets you say how fresh it is; a section/heading makes the citation human-readable. Without the span you can only name the document, not the sentence.

metadata-provenance.intro: Build chunk records that carry provenance, then filter retrieval to an allowed source set.
steps: Every chunk carries: id, text, source, char span, and an updated timestamp.
The span (start,end) is what lets you cite the EXACT passage, not just the document.
A metadata filter restricts retrieval to allowed sources/tenants/dates before ranking.
The timestamp is the hook for freshness/expiry handling later.
metadata-provenance.commonMistake: Storing metadata but never filtering on it — you attach source and tenant to each chunk, then search the whole index anyway, so a query can retrieve another tenant's document. Metadata you do not filter on is a leak waiting to happen.

metadata-provenance.text: Retrieval returns chunks, but an answer needs more than chunk text — it needs to be TRACEABLE and GOVERNABLE, and that comes from provenance metadata attached at ingestion. Model each chunk as a record: a stable id, the text, the SOURCE document id/title, the CHARACTER SPAN [start,end] within that source, and an UPDATED timestamp (plus any domain fields: tenant, access level, section heading). Each field earns its place. The span is what makes a real citation possible — you can quote and deep-link the exact sentence, not vaguely gesture at a document, which is the difference between "per your refund policy, section 3" and "the model says so." The source/tenant fields enable a METADATA FILTER: most vector stores let you constrain the search to chunks matching a predicate (source in allow-list, tenant = current user, updated > cutoff) BEFORE similarity ranking, which is both a relevance tool and a security boundary — cross-tenant retrieval is a data leak, and the filter is what prevents it. If you embedded chunks without it, the vectors are anonymous and you must re-ingest to recover source and span. So provenance is a required ingestion output, computed alongside the text, never bolted on after.

embeddings-intuition.unlock: You can define an embedding as a vector, say what "close" means, and explain why semantic search beats keyword match for paraphrases.

embeddings-intuition.doNotClaim: Don't claim embeddings "understand" text — they place text in a space where geometric closeness approximates meaning, which is powerful but not comprehension.

embeddings-intuition.text: A keyword search for "how do I get my money back?" returns nothing, because the policy page says "refunds are processed within 30 days" and shares no words with the query. The user gives up. Embeddings solve exactly this: they map both phrases to nearby points so the paraphrase matches. This lesson builds the intuition for why that works, using vectors you can compute by hand.

An embedding is a vector — a list of floating-point numbers — that represents a piece of text, and the DISTANCE between two vectors measures their relatedness (OpenAI's own definition). Text with similar meaning maps to nearby points; unrelated text maps far apart. This is what makes semantic search possible: instead of matching literal words, you embed the query and find the chunks whose vectors are closest. The magic (and the limit) is that "meaning" is approximated by geometry — the model learned to place related text together, but it is placing points in space, not reasoning.

embeddings-intuition.reveal: The representation must place semantically similar text at nearby points regardless of exact wording — so "money back" and "refund" get close vectors even with zero shared tokens. Embeddings provide this: distance encodes relatedness, so paraphrases retrieve each other. Keyword match only sees surface tokens and misses it.

embeddings-intuition.intro: Treat each item as a small fixed vector and find the nearest neighbor to a query vector by Euclidean distance.
steps: Each text becomes a vector; nearby vectors mean related meanings.
Distance (here Euclidean) quantifies "how related" — smaller is closer.
The nearest vector to the query is the most semantically related item.
This matches paraphrases keyword search would miss, because closeness is about meaning, not shared words.
embeddings-intuition.commonMistake: Comparing vectors of different dimensions, or assuming any two embedding models share a space. A vector from model A is meaningless distance-wise against a vector from model B — embeddings are only comparable within the same model and dimension.

embeddings-intuition.text: An embedding maps text to a fixed-length vector of floats, and the geometry of that space is the whole trick: the model was trained so that semantically related text lands at nearby points and unrelated text lands far apart. OpenAI states it plainly — "an embedding is a vector of floating point numbers; the distance between two vectors measures their relatedness." So "refund", "money back", and "reimbursement" cluster together even with no shared words, while "banana" sits in a different region. Semantic search exploits this directly: embed the query, then find the chunks whose vectors are nearest — retrieval by MEANING, not by literal token overlap, which is why it handles paraphrase, synonymy, and rephrasing that keyword search fails on. Two guardrails on the intuition. First, distance approximates relatedness; it does not mean the model "understands" — it is placing points, and it can place two things close for spurious reasons, which is why retrieval needs evaluation, not blind trust. Second, embeddings are only comparable within the same model and dimensionality: a vector has no meaning except relative to other vectors from the same model, so you cannot mix embedding models in one index or compare their distances. Get this picture — text as points, relatedness as closeness — and every later step (cosine similarity, top-k, thresholds) is just how you measure and rank that closeness.

storyboard.say: It starts with a question like "how do I get my money back?" — plain query text, no matching keywords in the policy.

Here's the trick: the model was trained so related meanings land nearby — "refund" and "money back" cluster even with no shared words.
We measure distance from the query point to find its nearest neighbor — the closest vector wins.
That nearest point is the matched chunk: the 30-day refund policy, retrieved by meaning, not by literal token overlap.
That's the whole insight — embed the query, find the nearest points, and paraphrase matches where keyword search returned nothing.

cosine-similarity.proof: A cosine-similarity function over hardcoded vectors that ranks candidates by angle, matching the hand-computed values.
cosine-similarity.unlock: You can write cosine = dot(a,b)/(|a||b|), state its range, and explain why normalized embeddings let you use a plain dot product.
cosine-similarity.outcome: Compute cosine similarity between vectors from first principles, and explain why it — not raw magnitude — is the recommended way to rank embedding relatedness.
cosine-similarity.doNotClaim: Don't claim cosine and Euclidean always agree — they give identical RANKINGS only when the vectors are normalized to length 1, which OpenAI embeddings are but arbitrary vectors are not.

cosine-similarity.text: Two chunks are equally relevant to a query, but one was extracted from a longer passage so its vector has a larger magnitude, and your magnitude-based scorer ranks it higher for the wrong reason. Cosine similarity ignores magnitude and compares only DIRECTION — the angle between vectors — which is what actually encodes meaning. This lesson makes the formula something you can compute and trust.

Cosine similarity is the standard relatedness metric for embeddings, and OpenAI explicitly recommends it. It is the cosine of the angle between two vectors: cos(θ) = (A · B) / (‖A‖‖B‖) — the dot product divided by the product of magnitudes. It ranges −1..1 for general vectors (1 = same direction, 0 = orthogonal, −1 = opposite) and 0..1 for the non-negative case. Crucially it measures DIRECTION, not length, so a chunk is not penalized or rewarded for the magnitude of its vector — only for how aligned its meaning is with the query.

cosine-similarity.prompt: Before reading: vector a=[1,0] and b=[10,0] point the same way but b is 10× longer. What is their cosine similarity, and what does that tell you?
cosine-similarity.reveal: cos = (1·10 + 0·0)/(1 · 10) = 10/10 = 1.0. Identical direction gives cosine 1 regardless of length — cosine ignores magnitude entirely. That is exactly why it is used for embeddings: relatedness is about direction (meaning), not how long the vector happens to be.

cosine-similarity.intro: Cosine similarity from its three parts: dot product, two magnitudes, divide.
steps: Dot product A·B sums the elementwise products.
Magnitude |A| = sqrt(A·A); divide the dot product by |A||B|.
Result is cos(θ): 1 = same direction, 0 = orthogonal, −1 = opposite.
Rank by highest cosine — it compares meaning-direction, ignoring vector length.
cosine-similarity.commonMistake: Dividing by only one magnitude (or forgetting to normalize) and calling it cosine. dot(a,b)/|a| is not cosine — you must divide by |a|·|b|. Skipping a magnitude lets long vectors dominate, reintroducing the magnitude bias cosine exists to remove.

cosine-similarity.text: Cosine similarity answers "how aligned are these two vectors?" and its formula follows directly from the geometric definition of the dot product: cos(θ) = (A · B) / (‖A‖‖B‖). Compute it in three steps — the dot product A·B (sum of elementwise products), the two magnitudes ‖A‖=sqrt(A·A) and ‖B‖, then divide. The value lives in [−1, 1] for general vectors: 1 means identical direction (maximally related), 0 means orthogonal (unrelated), −1 means opposite; for non-negative vectors it collapses to [0, 1]. The reason it is the default for embeddings — and OpenAI's explicit recommendation — is that it depends ONLY on direction, not magnitude. Meaning is encoded in which way a vector points, and two paraphrases can have different vector lengths for incidental reasons (passage length, term frequency); cosine cancels that out by dividing through the magnitudes, so a longer vector is never ranked higher just for being long. There is a performance corollary worth knowing: OpenAI embeddings are normalized to length 1, so ‖A‖=‖B‖=1 and cosine reduces to a plain dot product A·B — cheaper to compute — and, on normalized vectors, cosine and Euclidean distance produce IDENTICAL rankings. That equivalence only holds when vectors are unit-length; on arbitrary vectors, cosine and Euclidean can rank differently, so know whether your vectors are normalized before you shortcut the math.
cosine-similarity.title: Cosine ranks by angle, not by length
Cosine similarity = angle between vectors

That dot product alone is dangerous: a chunk from a longer passage has a bigger magnitude and inflates the raw score.
So we divide by the product of the magnitudes, cancelling length entirely and leaving only the angle between them.
The result is cos of theta in negative one to one: one means same direction, zero orthogonal, minus one opposite.
That length-free score ranks candidates by direction, so the truly relevant chunk wins no matter how long its passage was.

vector-stores-upsert.proof: An upsert function that inserts new chunk ids and overwrites existing ones by id, leaving no duplicates after re-ingesting a changed document.
vector-stores-upsert.unlock: You can explain what a vector store does and why upsert-by-id is the difference between a clean index and a duplicate-ridden one.
vector-stores-upsert.outcome: Use a vector store correctly: UPSERT chunks by stable id so re-ingesting a changed document replaces its vectors instead of creating duplicates.
vector-stores-upsert.doNotClaim: Don't claim insert and upsert are interchangeable — insert on re-ingest silently doubles your chunks and returns two copies of the same passage.

vector-stores-upsert.text: A doc gets edited and re-ingested nightly. A month later, retrieval returns the same sentence three times and the answer repeats itself — the pipeline used INSERT, so every re-ingest appended a fresh copy of every chunk instead of replacing the old one. The index is now 30× too big and full of stale duplicates. Upsert-by-id prevents this. This lesson makes the insert-vs-upsert distinction concrete.

A vector store holds {id, vector, metadata} records and answers nearest-neighbor queries over the vectors. The operation that keeps it healthy is UPSERT: write a record by its id — if the id exists, overwrite it; if not, insert it. This matters because RAG corpora change: documents get edited and re-ingested. If you INSERT on every ingest, you accumulate duplicate chunks (same content, new ids) that bloat the index and return repeated passages. If you upsert with a STABLE id derived from source+position, a re-ingest cleanly replaces the old vector with the new one.

vector-stores-upsert.prompt: Before reading: you re-ingest an edited document every night with INSERT. After 10 nights, how many copies of an unchanged paragraph are in the index?
vector-stores-upsert.reveal: Ten. INSERT appends new records each run, so an unchanged paragraph is stored 10 times (with 10 different auto-ids). Retrieval then returns the same passage repeatedly and the index is 10× too large. UPSERT with a stable id keyed on source+position would keep exactly one, overwriting it each night.

vector-stores-upsert.intro: A stable-id upsert: overwrite by id if present, insert if new — idempotent re-ingest.
steps: A vector store maps a stable id to {vector, text, metadata}.
Derive the id from source + position so the SAME chunk always gets the SAME id.
Upsert = set by id: overwrite when present, insert when new.
Re-ingesting a changed doc replaces its chunks in place — the index stays duplicate-free.
vector-stores-upsert.commonMistake: Generating a random/auto-increment id per chunk at ingest time. The id is different every run, so upsert can never find the old record to overwrite — it behaves like insert and you get duplicates. The id MUST be deterministic from the content's source+position.

vector-stores-upsert.text: A vector store is a keyed collection of {id, vector, metadata} that supports nearest-neighbor search, and the single most important discipline in using one is how you WRITE to it, because RAG corpora are living: documents get edited, republished, and re-ingested on a schedule. The write operation you want is UPSERT — write a record by id, overwriting if the id already exists and inserting if it does not — which makes re-ingestion IDEMPOTENT: running it twice on the same document leaves the index in the same state as running it once. The linchpin is a STABLE, DETERMINISTIC id: derive it from the source document id plus the chunk's position (or a content hash), so the exact same chunk always maps to the exact same id across runs. Then a nightly re-ingest of an edited doc overwrites precisely the chunks that changed and re-writes the rest identically — no growth, no stale copies. Contrast INSERT with an auto-generated id: every ingest appends fresh records, so an unchanged paragraph accumulates one duplicate per run, the index bloats linearly with time, and retrieval returns the same passage several times, wasting top-k slots and making answers repeat themselves. (A related operation, DELETE-by-id, handles removed content — when a document is deleted upstream, you must delete its chunk ids or they retrieve forever.) The mechanics are simple; the failure mode of getting them wrong is a silently degrading index, which is why upsert-by-stable-id is non-negotiable.
vector-stores-upsert.title: Upsert-by-stable-id makes re-ingestion idempotent
Upsert by stable id keeps the index clean
vector-stores-upsert.subtitle: same chunk -> same id -> overwrite, never duplicate

storyboard.say: A chunk arrives from re-ingestion, tagged by its source and position, ready to be written into the vector store.
Instead of blindly writing, we upsert — hand the chunk to the store and ask a single question first.
The decision that keeps the index clean: does a record with this exact id already exist in the store?
If yes, we overwrite the existing record in place — the edited chunk replaces its old copy, no duplicate created.
If no such id exists yet, we insert a fresh record — the chunk is genuinely new content.
Both branches write by the same stable id, so the store ends in one clean state either way.
The linchpin: a deterministic id from source plus position makes re-ingestion idempotent — run it twice, same index as once.

optionA.text: Overwrite each chunk in place by deterministic id. Idempotent, minimal writes, and unchanged chunks keep their id — but you must also delete ids that no longer exist in the new version.
optionA.label: Upsert by id

optionB.text: Remove every chunk for the source, then insert the new set. Simple and guarantees no orphans, but rewrites everything (more churn) and creates a window where the doc is missing from the index.
optionB.label: Delete-all + reinsert

vector-stores-upsert.guidance: Upsert by id (A) is the default: least churn, idempotent, and no availability gap. Its one gap — chunks that disappeared in the new version — you close with a delete of ids not present in the fresh set. Delete-all+reinsert (B) is acceptable for small documents where the rewrite is cheap and the momentary absence is tolerable.
vector-stores-upsert.question: On re-ingesting an edited document, delete-all-then-reinsert its chunks, or upsert by stable id?

options: So the same chunk maps to the same id every run, letting upsert overwrite the old record instead of inserting a duplicate.
Because nearest-neighbor search buckets vectors by id, so deterministic ids keep one document's chunks searchable together.
Because vector stores reject ids they cannot parse back to a source and position, and drop those writes silently.
So retrieval can group chunks by source, because upsert deduplicates by comparing ids as the results come back.
vector-stores-upsert.question: Why must a chunk's id be deterministic (source+position or content hash) for upsert to work?
vector-stores-upsert.explanation: Upsert overwrites by id. If the id changes every run (e.g. a random UUID), upsert can never locate the previous record, so it always inserts — reproducing the duplicate problem. A deterministic id ties each chunk to one stable record so re-ingest replaces rather than accumulates.

indexing-versioning.unlock: You can explain why vectors from two embedding models must never share an index and how a versioned rebuild swaps them safely.
indexing-versioning.outcome: Version an index so an embedding-model or chunking change rebuilds into a new namespace and swaps atomically, never mixing incompatible vectors in one searchable space.
indexing-versioning.doNotClaim: Don't claim you can "upgrade the embedding model in place" — new-model vectors are incomparable to old ones, so a partial migration silently corrupts every ranking.

indexing-versioning.text: A team upgrades the embedding model and re-embeds documents gradually into the SAME index. For a week, half the vectors are old-model and half new-model, their distances are not comparable, and retrieval quality collapses in ways nobody can reproduce. The fix is versioning: build the new embeddings into a separate index version and flip to it atomically. This lesson makes index versioning a first-class operation.

An index is tied to the exact embedding model and chunking scheme that produced its vectors, because distances are only meaningful WITHIN one model's space. So a change to the embedding model, its dimension, or your chunking strategy is not an edit — it is a REBUILD. The safe pattern is versioning: each build goes into its own namespace (e.g. docs@v2), you populate it fully in the background while v1 keeps serving, then atomically switch the ACTIVE pointer to v2. Queries always read the active version; a partially-built version is never served.

indexing-versioning.prompt: Before reading: you switch to a better embedding model and re-embed 50% of your docs into the existing index. Why does retrieval get WORSE, not better?
indexing-versioning.reveal: Because the index now mixes two incompatible vector spaces. A query embedded with the new model is compared by distance against both new-model vectors (comparable) and old-model vectors (not comparable) — the old ones produce garbage distances that can outrank the right answer. You cannot partially migrate an embedding model; you rebuild into a new version and swap.

indexing-versioning.intro: A version pointer: writes target the building version, reads target the active version, and you flip atomically.
steps: An index belongs to one embedding model + chunking scheme; changing either means a rebuild.
Build the new vectors into a SEPARATE version namespace while the old one serves.
Reads always target the ACTIVE version; the half-built version is invisible to queries.
Flip ACTIVE to the new version in one atomic step once the rebuild is complete.
indexing-versioning.commonMistake: Deleting the old index before the new one is fully built and verified. If the rebuild fails midway you have no serving index at all — always build-then-swap, and keep the previous version until the new one is validated so you can roll back.

indexing-versioning.text: Every vector in an index was produced by a specific embedding model at a specific dimension from chunks cut a specific way, and distances are only meaningful among vectors from the SAME model — so the model+chunking is effectively part of the index's identity. That makes certain changes fundamentally different from ordinary upserts: swapping the embedding model, changing its output dimension, or altering your chunking strategy invalidates every existing vector at once. You cannot migrate these in place, because during the migration the index holds a mixture of two incomparable spaces and a query compared against both gets nonsense distances from the wrong-model half, silently corrupting rankings. The correct operation is a VERSIONED REBUILD: allocate a new namespace (docs@v2), re-chunk and re-embed the whole corpus into it in the background while v1 continues serving live traffic, VALIDATE the new version (spot-check retrieval quality, run your recall@k eval), then flip a single ACTIVE pointer from v1 to v2 atomically so no request ever sees a partially-built index. Keep v1 around after the swap so you can roll back instantly if v2 regresses. This is the same build-then-swap discipline as a blue/green deploy, applied to a search index: reads target the active version, writes target the building version, and the cutover is one atomic step. Ordinary content edits still use upsert within the active version; versioning is reserved for changes that break vector comparability.

The rebuild runs in the background, populating index v2 completely while v1 keeps serving live traffic untouched.

Only when validation passes do you atomically flip the ACTIVE pointer from v1 to v2 — one instant switch, no half-migrated state.
After the swap, every query reads from v2 alone. The index is never a mix of two incomparable spaces.
The insight: distances only mean anything within one model's space, so you build the new space fully, then swap — never migrate in place.

indexing-versioning.symptom: Right after an embedding-model upgrade, retrieval returns wildly irrelevant chunks that were fine yesterday.

optionA.text: Build the new index alongside the old, validate, then flip. No mixed spaces, zero-downtime cutover, instant rollback — at the cost of temporarily storing two index copies.
optionA.label: Versioned rebuild + swap

optionB.text: Overwrite vectors in the existing index as you go. Saves storage, but during the migration the index mixes two models' vectors and every ranking is corrupted until it finishes.
optionB.label: Re-embed in place

indexing-versioning.guidance: Always versioned rebuild + swap (A). The temporary double storage is cheap insurance against serving a mixed-space index, which produces unreproducible quality collapse and has no safe rollback. In-place re-embedding (B) is only defensible if you can take the index fully offline during the rebuild — which usually costs more than the extra storage.
indexing-versioning.question: Upgrading the embedding model: rebuild into a new version and atomically swap, or re-embed in place to save storage?

options: Because holding both models' vectors doubles the index size, and most vector stores reject further writes once that ceiling is hit.
Because distances between vectors from different models are not comparable, so a mixed index returns corrupted rankings.
Because the new model embeds more slowly, so queries touching re-embedded chunks time out until the migration finishes.
Because upsert cannot change a vector's dimension in place, so re-embedded chunks land as duplicates beside the old ones.
indexing-versioning.question: Why can't you gradually migrate to a new embedding model within the same index?
indexing-versioning.explanation: Each model defines its own vector space; a distance is only meaningful between vectors from the same model. A half-migrated index compares the query against both spaces, and the wrong-model vectors yield meaningless distances that can outrank correct results — so you rebuild into a new version and swap atomically instead.

top-k-thresholds.proof: A top-k selector plus a threshold gate that passes strong retrievals through and returns a refusal when the top score falls under the threshold, tested on both cases.
top-k-thresholds.unlock: You can implement top-k, explain why it always returns SOMETHING, and why a threshold is what stops the model from answering off irrelevant chunks.
top-k-thresholds.outcome: Rank candidates by similarity and take the top-k, then gate on a minimum similarity τ: when the best chunk scores below τ, return "refuse: no supported context" instead of grounding on weak evidence.
top-k-thresholds.doNotClaim: Don't claim top-k alone prevents bad answers — it returns the k best even when the best is terrible, so without a threshold the model grounds on noise and hallucinates confidently.

top-k-thresholds.text: A user asks something your corpus simply does not cover. Top-k dutifully returns its three "best" chunks — all scoring 0.11, all irrelevant — and the model, handed irrelevant context, invents a plausible-sounding answer. The system had no way to say "I don't have this." A similarity threshold is that way. This lesson builds the refusal gate that turns weak retrieval into an honest "no".

Top-k has a blind spot: it ALWAYS returns k chunks, even for a query the corpus cannot answer, because "the best 3 of a bad set" are still returned. The fix is a THRESHOLD τ on the top similarity score: if the highest-scoring retrieved chunk is below τ, the retrieval is too weak to ground an answer, so the system should REFUSE ("no supported context") rather than feed the model noise. This is the retrieval-side half of the grounding contract you will formalize in Module 4 — better an honest refusal than a confident hallucination built on a 0.11-similarity chunk.

top-k-thresholds.prompt: Before reading: for an out-of-corpus question, top-k returns 3 chunks all scoring 0.10. What should the system do, and what will it do WITHOUT a threshold?
top-k-thresholds.reveal: It should refuse: no chunk is similar enough to support an answer, so grounding is impossible. Without a threshold, it passes those 0.10-scoring chunks as "context" and the model produces a confident answer grounded in nothing relevant — a hallucination. The threshold converts weak retrieval into a refusal instead of a guess.

top-k-thresholds.intro: Rank candidates, take the top-k, then check the top score against τ and refuse when retrieval is too weak.
steps: Top-k is a sorted cut: rank candidates by score descending (deterministic tiebreak) and take k.
k is a recall/noise dial — too small misses evidence at rank k+1, too large adds prompt noise.
Then compare the TOP score to a threshold τ chosen from your score distribution.
If best < τ: refuse — no context is strong enough to ground an answer. If best ≥ τ: ground on chunks clearing τ.
top-k-thresholds.commonMistake: Copying a threshold value from a tutorial. τ depends on your embedding model and score distribution — a good τ for one model is meaningless for another. Calibrate τ from a labeled set (scores of known-relevant vs known-irrelevant chunks), do not hardcode a borrowed number.

top-k-thresholds.text: Top-k answers "which chunks are most similar?" but never "is the most similar one actually good enough?" — and that gap is where hallucinations enter, because top-k returns its k best even when every candidate is irrelevant. A similarity THRESHOLD τ closes the gap: after ranking, compare the TOP score to τ, and if even the best chunk falls below it, the retrieval is too weak to support any grounded answer, so the system returns a REFUSAL ("no supported context") instead of handing the model noise. This is a deliberate design choice that an honest RAG system must make: for a question outside the corpus, the right output is "I don't have information on that," not a fluent fabrication built on a 0.11-similarity chunk. Two details make it work in practice. First, τ is CALIBRATED, not guessed: it depends on the embedding model and the query/corpus, so you set it from data — look at the score distribution of known-relevant chunks versus known-irrelevant ones and pick a τ that separates them, then verify the refusal rate is sane (too high τ refuses answerable questions; too low lets noise through). Second, you can apply τ twice: as a REFUSAL gate on the top score (refuse the whole query if nothing clears it) and as a FILTER within top-k (drop individual chunks below τ so even a grounded answer never includes weak evidence). The threshold is the retrieval-side enforcement of the grounding contract — the mechanism that lets the system say no.
top-k-thresholds.title: A threshold converts weak retrieval into an honest refusal

top-k-thresholds.subtitle: top score below τ -> refuse instead of grounding on noise

storyboard.say: Retrieval hands us its top-k ranked chunks — but top-k always returns k, even when every candidate is weak.
Before grounding, we inspect the single top score and ask the gate one question: is the best chunk actually good enough?
If the top score clears the threshold tau, we pass — the retrieval is strong enough to trust.
We keep only the chunks at or above tau, then hand that qualifying context to the model to ground its answer.
But if even the best chunk falls below tau, the gate refuses: no supported context, rather than feeding the model noise.
That refusal branch is the whole point — for a question outside the corpus, honest silence beats a fluent fabrication.

Either way, calibrate τ from labeled relevant/irrelevant scores and monitor both the refusal rate and the hallucination rate; do not pick τ by feel.

top-k-thresholds.explanation: Top-k is purely relative — "the best k of whatever exists" — with no absolute quality bar. For an unanswerable query it still returns 3 low-scoring chunks, and the model treats them as context. A similarity threshold adds the absolute bar: if the best score is below τ, refuse.

hybrid-search.proof: A Reciprocal Rank Fusion function that merges a BM25-style list and a vector list into one ranking using 1/(rank+k).
hybrid-search.unlock: You can explain what each retriever misses alone and why RRF fuses on rank position to sidestep incompatible score scales.
hybrid-search.outcome: Combine keyword (lexical) and vector (semantic) retrieval so exact-term matches and paraphrase matches both surface — fusing two ranked lists by rank, not by incomparable raw scores.
hybrid-search.doNotClaim: Don't claim vector search subsumes keyword search — it misses exact identifiers, codes, and rare terms that lexical search nails; hybrid exists because each covers the other's blind spot.

hybrid-search.text: A user searches for error code "E-4021" and gets nothing useful: vector search finds semantically "similar" prose but not the exact code, because rare alphanumeric tokens embed poorly. Meanwhile "how do I get money back" fails on pure keyword search. Each retriever has a blind spot exactly where the other is strong. Hybrid search runs both and fuses them. This lesson builds the fusion correctly, on ranks.

Two retrieval families cover different query types. LEXICAL search (BM25) matches literal tokens — unbeatable for exact identifiers, product codes, rare terms, and names. VECTOR search matches meaning — unbeatable for paraphrases and synonyms. HYBRID search runs both in parallel and fuses their ranked lists. The catch is that their scores are not comparable (BM25 is unbounded; cosine is roughly 0–1), so you cannot average them. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), used by systems like Azure AI Search, solves this by fusing on RANK POSITION: each doc gets 1/(rank + k) per list (k≈60), and the per-list scores are summed — raw scores are ignored entirely.

hybrid-search.prompt: Before reading: you want to combine a BM25 list (scores like 12.4, 8.1) and a vector list (scores like 0.82, 0.61). Why is averaging the two scores a bad idea?
hybrid-search.reveal: The scales are incomparable: BM25 is unbounded and can be tens or hundreds; cosine is ~0–1. Averaging lets the larger-magnitude BM25 score dominate regardless of true relevance. RRF avoids this by discarding raw scores and fusing on RANK position instead — 1/(rank+k) summed across lists — so a #1 in either list contributes the same amount.

hybrid-search.intro: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: convert each list to reciprocal-rank scores and sum per document.
steps: Run lexical (BM25) and vector search separately; each returns a ranked list of ids.
For each list, a document's contribution is 1/(k + its 1-based rank), k≈60.
Sum a document's reciprocal-rank scores across all lists it appears in.
Sort by the summed score — documents ranked high in BOTH lists rise to the top.
hybrid-search.commonMistake: Using 0-based ranks in 1/(k+rank). With rank 0 the top item gets 1/k, and it distorts the intended weighting; RRF assumes 1-based ranks so the first result is 1/(k+1). Off-by-one here quietly changes the fusion.

hybrid-search.text: Hybrid search exists because lexical and semantic retrieval fail in opposite places: BM25 (lexical) matches literal tokens and dominates on exact identifiers, error codes, rare terms, and proper names, but is blind to paraphrase; vector search matches meaning and handles rephrasing and synonyms, but embeds rare alphanumeric tokens poorly and can miss an exact-string query. Running both and combining them covers each blind spot — but naive combination fails because their score scales are INCOMPATIBLE: BM25 scores are unbounded positive numbers while cosine similarities sit near 0–1, so averaging or summing raw scores lets the larger-magnitude side dominate arbitrarily. Reciprocal Rank Fusion sidesteps this entirely by throwing away the raw scores and fusing on RANK POSITION. Each document gets a reciprocal-rank contribution of 1/(k + rank) from each list it appears in (rank is 1-based; k is a constant, and Azure AI Search notes experiments favor k≈60), and a document's final score is the SUM of these contributions across lists. Because only positions matter, a #1 result contributes the same 1/(k+1) whether it came from BM25 or the vector index — the incomparable scales never meet. The effect is that documents ranked highly in BOTH retrievers rise to the top of the fused list (agreement is rewarded), while a document strong in only one list still gets partial credit. Note the k in RRF is unrelated to the k in top-k; it is a smoothing constant that flattens the gap between top ranks. RRF is the standard, score-scale-free way to make hybrid retrieval work.
hybrid-search.title: RRF fuses ranked lists by position, not by score
Hybrid search via Reciprocal Rank Fusion
hybrid-search.subtitle: two ranked lists fused by 1/(k+rank), scores ignored

optionA.text: Run BM25 + vector and fuse on rank. Catches exact codes AND paraphrases; agreement between retrievers boosts confidence. Costs two searches plus a fusion step.

optionB.label: Pure vector

hybrid-search.guidance: If your queries include exact identifiers, SKUs, error codes, or names alongside natural language, go hybrid (A) — the extra search is worth catching the queries pure vector (B) silently fails on. For a corpus and query mix that is entirely conversational prose, pure vector is a reasonable, cheaper default. Measure recall@k on BOTH query types before deciding.
hybrid-search.question: For a corpus with both natural-language questions and exact product codes, use pure vector search or hybrid (RRF)?

options: Because ranks are integers, so summing them avoids the floating-point rounding that corrupts fused score totals.

reranking.text: First-stage vector search returns 20 plausible chunks, but the single most on-point one sits at rank 8, so with top-3 it never reaches the model. The bi-encoder embedding is fast but coarse; it got the neighborhood right and the ordering wrong. A reranker rescores those 20 candidates with a sharper relevance model and lifts the true best to rank 1. This lesson builds the two-stage retrieve-then-rerank pipeline.

Production retrieval is usually TWO stages. Stage one (retrieval) is cheap and wide: embed the query, pull the top N candidates (N large, e.g. 50–100) by cosine — fast because the vectors are precomputed, but the ranking is coarse. Stage two (reranking) is expensive and narrow: a stronger model scores query-document RELEVANCE for each of those N candidates and reorders them, then you keep the top k. The division of labor is deliberate: you cannot afford the expensive scorer over the whole corpus, so first-stage retrieval narrows millions of chunks to a candidate set, and reranking spends its budget precisely where it matters — ordering the finalists.

What it cannot fix: if the right chunk had NOT been in the 20 candidates at all, reranking never sees it — reranking reorders the candidate set, it does not search the corpus. First-stage recall bounds what reranking can achieve.

reranking.text: Reranking exists because there is a fundamental cost/quality split in relevance scoring. The fast first-stage retriever (a bi-encoder: query and documents embedded independently, compared by cosine) is cheap enough to run over millions of chunks because the document vectors are precomputed — but that independence makes it coarse; it gets the right neighborhood but often the wrong order. A reranker (typically a cross-encoder that reads the query and a candidate TOGETHER) produces a much sharper relevance judgment, but it must run per candidate at query time and so cannot be applied to the whole corpus. The pattern resolves the tension: STAGE 1 casts a wide, cheap net — retrieve a large candidate set (N of 50–100) by cosine, optimizing for RECALL (get the right chunk anywhere in the set) — and STAGE 2 spends the expensive scorer only on those N finalists, optimizing for PRECISION (order them well) and keeping the final top-k. Two consequences define correct use. First, reranking cannot exceed first-stage recall: it only reorders what retrieval already surfaced, so if the answer chunk was not in the candidate set, no reranker recovers it — which is why N must be generous. Second, the reranker is where you spend quality budget to fix the "right chunk at rank 8" problem that top-k alone drops. The result is better than either stage alone: cheap wide retrieval you could not get from the reranker's cost, and precise ordering you could not get from the bi-encoder's coarseness.

query-rewriting.text: In a chat, the user asks "what is your refund window?" then follows up "and what about theirs?" The second query, embedded verbatim, retrieves nothing useful — "what about theirs?" has no content to match. The missing context ("theirs" = the competitor's refund policy) lives in the conversation, not the query. Query rewriting reconstructs a self-contained query before retrieval. This lesson builds that rewrite step.

The retriever embeds whatever query you give it, and a raw conversational turn is often a terrible query: it is underspecified ("what about theirs?"), full of unresolved pronouns ("it", "that one"), or too terse to embed meaningfully. QUERY REWRITING sits between the user and the retriever and transforms the query into something that retrieves well — most importantly COREFERENCE RESOLUTION (replace pronouns/ellipsis with their referents from conversation history) and EXPANSION (add synonyms or implied terms). The rewritten query is what gets embedded and searched; the original is still shown to the user.

Embedded alone it matches generic chunks about "annual" anything. Rewriting it to "annual plan price" using the prior turn gives the retriever real terms to match.

query-rewriting.commonMistake: Rewriting away the user's actual intent — over-expanding or "correcting" the query so it retrieves something plausible but not what they asked. A rewrite must preserve intent; adding unrelated terms drags retrieval toward the wrong chunks. Resolve references, don't invent new questions.

query-rewriting.text: Retrieval quality is bounded by the query you hand the embedder, and in a conversation the raw user turn is frequently a poor query — a fact that is easy to miss because the HUMAN understands the follow-up perfectly from context the retriever never sees. "What about theirs?", "and the annual one?", "does it apply to that?" are all crippled as retrieval queries: they are underspecified, pronoun-laden, or elliptical, so embedding them verbatim produces a vector with little relevant content, and the retriever returns generic or wrong chunks. QUERY REWRITING is the transform that fixes the query string before it reaches the retriever. The two highest-value rewrites are COREFERENCE RESOLUTION — replace pronouns and ellipsis ("theirs", "it", "the annual one") with their explicit referents drawn from conversation history, producing a self-contained query — and EXPANSION — add synonyms or implied terms so a terse query has more surface for semantic matching. (Related techniques include decomposing a multi-part question into sub-queries and, in some systems, generating a hypothetical answer to embed instead of the question.) The discipline is that a rewrite must PRESERVE INTENT: the goal is to say what the user meant more explicitly, not to substitute a different, easier-to-retrieve question — over-expansion that injects unrelated terms pulls retrieval off target, which is its own failure mode. In the pipeline, the rewritten query is what gets embedded and searched, while the original user text is kept for display, logging, and the final answer's framing. Rewriting improves the FIRST stage of retrieval at its source: better query in, better candidates out, which then feed top-k and reranking.

grounding-contract.proof: A verifier that checks each answer claim against the retrieved context and flags any claim with no supporting chunk as ungrounded.

grounding-contract.text: A RAG answer looks perfect: it cites the retrieved policy AND adds a helpful extra detail — "and refunds include original shipping." That last clause is nowhere in the context; the model added it from its training data. It reads as authoritative and it is wrong. Grounding is not "context was present" — it is "every claim is supported by the context." This lesson makes the grounding contract an enforceable check.

The whole point of RAG is that answers are GROUNDED in retrieved text you control. But putting context in the prompt does not force the model to stay within it — models blend retrieved context with parametric knowledge and can emit claims the context never supported. The GROUNDING CONTRACT is the rule that makes RAG trustworthy: the answer may assert ONLY what the retrieved chunks support; any claim without a supporting chunk is a contract violation and must be removed, flagged, or trigger a refusal. Enforcing it means VERIFYING claims against context, which is the foundation for citations (next) and faithfulness scoring (Module 5).

A grounded answer requires EVERY claim to trace to context. A partly-grounded answer with one invented clause is a contract violation, and the invented clause is exactly the dangerous kind of hallucination because the rest is correct.

grounding-contract.text: The grounding contract is the rule that separates a trustworthy RAG answer from a fluent guess: the model may assert only what the retrieved context supports, so EVERY claim in the answer must trace to a retrieved chunk. The reason this needs enforcement — rather than trust — is that supplying context does not constrain the model to it. Language models blend the prompt's retrieved text with their parametric knowledge, and they will happily emit a claim that "sounds right" but appears in no chunk, especially when it is adjacent to correct, grounded claims. That mixed answer is the most dangerous failure mode: the grounded parts lend authority to the ungrounded insertion. Enforcing the contract is therefore a VERIFICATION step, not a prompting hope. Decompose the answer into atomic claims; for each claim, check whether the retrieved context supports it; and treat the answer as grounded only if every claim passes. An unsupported claim is a contract violation with three possible responses: remove the claim, flag it for review, or — if the core of the answer is unsupported — refuse. This per-claim framing is exactly what the next two ideas build on: CITATIONS attach the supporting chunk/span to each grounded claim (making the trace explicit and user-visible), and the FAITHFULNESS metric in Module 5 is literally the fraction of claims that are supported. Grounding is not "was context present" or "did the answer mention a source"; it is the auditable property that no claim exceeds the evidence.

First, cite PER CLAIM, not per answer: a multi-claim answer draws from multiple chunks, so each claim must carry the citation of the chunk that actually supports IT — citing the top-ranked chunk for every claim mis-attributes evidence and quietly breaks verifiability. Second, a claim you cannot map to any supporting chunk is, by definition, not citable — and an uncitable claim is an ungrounded claim, so it must be dropped or trigger a refusal, never shipped with a fabricated or nearest-guess citation. refusal-when-unsupported.text: A compliance bot is asked about a regulation your documents do not cover. Retrieval returns weakly-related chunks, grounding finds no claim it can support, and yet the system stitches together an answer anyway — which is confidently wrong in a domain where wrong is expensive. The correct output was "I don't have information on that regulation." This lesson makes refusal an explicit, testable branch, not an accident.

Earlier lessons gave you two refusal triggers: the retrieval THRESHOLD (best similarity below τ) and the grounding contract (no claim is supported). This lesson unifies them into a single decision at answer time: does the retrieved, cited context actually COVER the question? If yes, answer and cite. If no — nothing cleared τ, or no answer claim can be grounded/cited — REFUSE with an honest message. Refusal is a designed outcome: in RAG, "I don't know" backed by "nothing in the corpus supports this" is more valuable than a fabricated answer, especially in high-stakes domains.

An always-answer system fabricates when the corpus lacks the answer, and in legal/medical/financial domains a confident fabrication causes real harm. A system that refuses out-of-corpus questions ("I don't have information on that") fails safe — the user knows to look elsewhere instead of trusting a hallucination.

refusal-when-unsupported.text: A trustworthy RAG system must be able to say "I don't know," and it must do so on purpose. Two earlier mechanisms already detect insufficiency: the retrieval THRESHOLD refuses when the best chunk's similarity is below τ (nothing relevant was found), and the grounding contract flags an answer whose claims cannot be supported by context. This lesson unifies them into one answer-time DECISION: does the retrieved, cited context actually COVER what the question asks? Define coverage against the question's required aspects and set a floor — often "every required aspect must be supported by cited context" — and only answer when the floor is met; otherwise refuse with an honest, specific message ("I don't have information on that in my sources"). The reframing that matters is cultural as much as technical: refusal is a FEATURE. For out-of-corpus questions, the alternatives to refusal are a wrong answer or a fabricated one, and in high-stakes domains (legal, medical, financial, compliance) those are worse than an honest non-answer that tells the user to look elsewhere — a false refusal costs a little friction, a confident hallucination costs trust and possibly harm. Because refusal is a designed branch, it must be TESTED like any other output: include known-unanswerable questions in your eval set and assert the system refuses them, or the branch silently rots and the system regresses to always-answering. The refusal decision belongs at the seam between grounding and generation — after retrieval and grounding have reported what the context can support, and before you commit to an answer.

stale-chunk-handling.proof: A freshness filter that drops chunks older than a TTL and, among survivors, keeps the newest version when duplicates conflict.
stale-chunk-handling.unlock: You can explain why an index without freshness handling serves stale facts and how the timestamp metadata prevents it.
stale-chunk-handling.outcome: Use the ingest/updated timestamp to keep retrieval fresh: filter out expired chunks and prefer newer content when two chunks conflict.
stale-chunk-handling.doNotClaim: Don't claim re-ingestion alone keeps content fresh — if the old chunk is never expired or superseded, retrieval can still surface last quarter's policy next to this quarter's.

stale-chunk-handling.text: A policy changed from a 14-day to a 30-day refund window. The new chunk was upserted, but an OLD chunk from a different source page still says 14 days, and retrieval sometimes surfaces the stale one — so the bot gives two different answers depending on the query. The index has no notion of freshness. Timestamps on chunks, plus a filter that expires and supersedes them, fix this. This lesson makes freshness a retrieval-time rule.

Documents change, and an index that never accounts for time will happily serve outdated facts alongside current ones. The provenance TIMESTAMP you stored at ingestion (Module 1) is the hook for freshness: at retrieval you can (1) EXPIRE chunks older than a time-to-live so obsolete content is never returned, and (2) SUPERSEDE — when two retrieved chunks cover the same fact but conflict, prefer the one with the newer timestamp. Without this, upserting a corrected chunk is not enough: a stale duplicate from another source can still outrank or accompany it.

stale-chunk-handling.prompt: Before reading: you upsert a corrected policy chunk, but retrieval still sometimes returns the old value. The corrected chunk exists — so why does the stale one appear?
stale-chunk-handling.reveal: Because the stale value lives in a DIFFERENT chunk (e.g. another page or an old snapshot) that was never expired or superseded. Upserting the corrected chunk only updates that one id; it does not remove or down-rank other chunks stating the old fact. You need a freshness rule — expire by TTL and, on conflict, prefer the newer timestamp — to stop the stale chunk from surfacing.

stale-chunk-handling.intro: Filter out expired chunks, then resolve conflicts by keeping the newest.
steps: Every chunk carries an updated timestamp from ingestion.
Expire: drop any chunk older than the TTL before it can be retrieved.
Supersede: when two surviving chunks state the same fact, keep the newer one.
Upserting a correction is necessary but not sufficient — you must also expire/supersede stale duplicates.
stale-chunk-handling.commonMistake: Using a single global TTL for all content. A product price may go stale in days while a founding-date fact never expires; one TTL either expires evergreen content too soon or lets volatile content rot. Set TTL per content type (or per source), not one number for the whole index.

stale-chunk-handling.text: An index is a snapshot that drifts out of date as the world changes, and nothing about vector similarity knows or cares that a chunk is stale — a two-year-old policy embeds just as strongly as today's. Freshness must therefore be enforced explicitly at retrieval, using the UPDATED timestamp you attached to every chunk at ingestion. Two mechanisms cover it. EXPIRY: apply a time-to-live so chunks older than the TTL are filtered out before ranking and can never surface — this is how you guarantee obsolete content leaves the answer set. SUPERSEDING: when retrieval returns two chunks that speak to the same fact but disagree (the classic "14 days" vs "30 days" from different pages), resolve the conflict by keeping the one with the NEWER timestamp, so the current value wins. The key insight, and a common production surprise, is that UPSERTING a corrected chunk is not enough on its own: upsert updates one id, but the stale value often lives in a different chunk — another source page, an old crawl snapshot, a duplicate — that upsert never touched, so it keeps surfacing until expiry or superseding removes it. Two refinements make this practical: TTL should be PER CONTENT TYPE (volatile prices expire fast; evergreen facts may never expire — a single global TTL is wrong for both), and expiry should ideally trigger re-ingestion of the source rather than just deletion, so freshness is a refresh loop, not a slow erosion of coverage. Freshness turns the passive timestamp metadata into an active guarantee that grounding uses current evidence.

The insight: freshness must be enforced at retrieval — expire old chunks, supersede conflicts — because the index will never do it for you.

recall-at-k.text: A team keeps tweaking prompts to fix wrong answers, but the real cause is retrieval: the relevant chunk is not in the top-k for 40% of queries. They cannot see it because they only look at final answers. Recall@k exposes it directly — a labeled set says which chunks SHOULD be retrieved, and the metric reports how often they are. This lesson makes retrieval quality a measurable number you can optimize.

You cannot improve what you cannot measure, and in RAG the retrieval stage is measured separately from the answer. RECALL@K is the workhorse metric: over a labeled evaluation set (queries each tagged with their relevant chunk ids), it computes the fraction of relevant chunks that appear in the retrieved top-k, averaged across queries. It isolates retrieval — did the right chunks come back? — from generation, so when answers are bad you can tell whether the problem is retrieval (fix chunking, k, embeddings, hybrid, reranking) or grounding (fix the prompt/contract). RAGAS defines the analogous LLM-based context recall as the fraction of reference claims supported by the retrieved context.

recall-at-k.text: RAG has two failure surfaces — retrieval (were the right chunks found?) and generation (was the answer faithful to them?) — and you cannot fix either without measuring them separately. Recall@k measures the FIRST. On a labeled evaluation set where each query is annotated with the chunk ids that genuinely answer it, recall@k for a query is |relevant ∩ top-k| / |relevant|: of the chunks that SHOULD have been retrieved, what fraction actually appeared in the top-k? Average that over the set and you have a single number for how well retrieval surfaces the evidence, independent of what the model then does with it. This isolation is the whole point. If final answers are poor, recall@k tells you WHERE to look: low recall@k means the right chunk often is not even reaching the model, so the fix is in the retrieval stack — chunking, k, the embedding model, hybrid search, reranking — and no amount of prompt engineering will help. High recall@k with bad answers points the other way, to grounding and generation. Two things to hold precisely: the denominator is the number of RELEVANT chunks, not k and not the number retrieved (that error silently inflates or deflates the metric); and recall@k rises monotonically with k (larger k can only capture more relevant chunks), which is exactly why you report it AT a specific k that matches what you actually feed the model, and pair it with a noise/precision view so you do not "win" recall by ballooning k. RAGAS formalizes a claim-level cousin — context recall as the fraction of reference claims supported by the retrieved context — but the discipline is the same: a labeled truth, a fraction captured, a number you optimize.

answer-faithfulness.text: Retrieval is great — recall@k is 0.95 — yet users report the bot "makes things up." The problem is downstream: the model retrieves the right context and then adds claims that context never supported. Recall@k cannot see this; it measures retrieval, not the answer. Faithfulness does: it scores what fraction of the answer's claims the context actually backs. This lesson makes that generation-side quality a number.

Recall@k measures retrieval; FAITHFULNESS measures generation. RAGAS defines it precisely: faithfulness is the number of claims in the response supported by the retrieved context divided by the total number of claims in the response, on a 0..1 scale — a response is fully faithful when all its claims can be supported by the retrieved context. It operationalizes the grounding contract as a SCORE: decompose the answer into atomic claims, check each against the context, and report the supported fraction. A faithfulness below 1.0 means the answer asserted something the evidence did not support — the exact failure the grounding contract forbids.

A perfectly faithful answer scores 1.0 — every claim supported. The 0.75 flags that one claim exceeded the evidence, which is precisely what you want to catch and drive to zero.

answer-faithfulness.commonMistake: Confusing faithfulness with correctness. Faithfulness asks "is the claim supported by the RETRIEVED CONTEXT?", not "is the claim true in the world?". An answer can be faithful to wrong context (garbage in) or unfaithful while accidentally true — faithfulness measures adherence to the evidence, which is a distinct axis from factual correctness.

answer-faithfulness.text: Faithfulness is the metric that turns the grounding contract into a number for the GENERATION stage, complementing recall@k on the retrieval stage. RAGAS defines it exactly: faithfulness = (claims in the response supported by the retrieved context) / (total claims in the response), scored 0..1, with 1.0 meaning every claim in the answer can be supported by the retrieved context. Computing it follows the grounding contract's shape — decompose the answer into atomic claims, and for each claim judge whether the retrieved context supports it — but reports the SUPPORTED FRACTION rather than a pass/fail, which makes it trackable over time and comparable across pipeline changes. The critical distinction, and the source of most confusion, is that faithfulness measures adherence to the EVIDENCE, not truth in the world: a claim is faithful if the retrieved context backs it, regardless of whether the context itself is correct. This means faithfulness and correctness are orthogonal — an answer can be perfectly faithful to a stale or wrong chunk (which is why the freshness and retrieval-quality work upstream matters), or it can be unfaithful yet accidentally true. You want faithfulness because it isolates the one failure the model uniquely introduces: drifting beyond the provided evidence, i.e. hallucinating additions even when the right context was retrieved. Read together, the two metrics diagnose any RAG failure — low recall@k means the evidence was not retrieved (fix retrieval); high recall@k with low faithfulness means the evidence was there but the answer exceeded it (fix generation: tighten the prompt, enforce the contract, drop or refuse unsupported claims). A production RAG system tracks both on a labeled set and treats a faithfulness regression as seriously as a broken test.

rag-cost-latency.text: A RAG feature ships, and the bill triples versus the old bare-LLM version while p95 latency doubles. Nobody budgeted the pipeline: each request now embeds the query, searches, reranks, AND stuffs k chunks of context into the prompt as paid input tokens. Raising k for recall quietly multiplied the token cost. This lesson makes RAG's cost and latency an explicit budget, not a surprise.

RAG is not free relative to a bare LLM call — it adds both LATENCY (embed the query, search the index, optionally rerank, all before generation) and COST (the retrieved context is INPUT tokens you pay for on every call, on top of the embedding cost). The central tension is that the same knob that raises recall — a bigger k — directly multiplies injected context tokens, so cost and prompt size scale with k. Production RAG treats this as a budget: estimate the added latency per stage and the token cost of the context, and choose k where recall is adequate and cost/latency are acceptable.

rag-cost-latency.text: Every architectural choice has a bill, and RAG's is paid in two currencies relative to a bare LLM call. LATENCY: before the model generates a single token, a RAG request must embed the (possibly rewritten) query, search the vector index for candidates, and — if you rerank — run a second-stage scorer over them; these stages are sequential and add to time-to-first-token. COST: the retrieved context does not appear by magic in the prompt — it is INPUT TOKENS, billed on every single call, on top of the (usually small) per-query embedding cost. The two combine into the central RAG tradeoff, because the knob you reach for to improve recall — a larger k — is exactly the knob that inflates both: context tokens = k × tokens-per-chunk, so cost and prompt size grow LINEARLY with k, and a bigger prompt adds some processing latency too. This is why "just raise k until answers are good" is a trap: it silently multiplies your recurring token bill across all traffic and can even hurt quality via distraction. Production RAG treats cost/latency as an explicit budget you compute: estimate per-stage latency and the per-request context-token cost at a candidate k, then pick the SMALLEST k that hits your recall@k target, using reranking (spend once to order well) rather than a huge k (pay forever for a noisy prompt) when ranking is the real problem. Levers that lower the bill without sacrificing recall include tighter chunks (fewer tokens per chunk), caching frequent query results, and filtering with metadata to shrink the candidate set — but the first discipline is simply MEASURING the two currencies so raising k is a decision, not an accident.
